source_refs.note: Topic 11.9 with the conjugated dienes scheme and Quick Check 11.10, printed page 265.

blocks.text: As the name indicates, a diene is a molecule containing two double bonds between carbon atoms. In a Conjugated diene, the double bonds in the carbon chain are separated by a single bond. The adjacent double bonds in conjugated dienes allow for the overlap of p-orbitals on three or more adjacent atoms. This overlap leads to a delocalization of electrons, which can stabilize the molecule and affect its reactivity. In conjugated dienes pi-bond overlap extends over the entire system.

blocks.alt: CH2=CH-CH=CH2, but-1,3-diene; CH2=C(CH3)-CH=CH2 with the CH3 above the second carbon, 2-methylbut-1,3-diene (isoprene); and a chain C-C-C-C with a p orbital lobe above and below each carbon joined by wavy lines above and below, labelled Delocalization of pi electrons of the conjugated bonds.
blocks.caption: Conjugated dienes and delocalization of pi electrons (original drawing after the scheme printed on p265 of the textbook).

blocks.text: Conjugated alkenes are an important class of compounds in organic chemistry, featuring unique properties due to the arrangement of their double bonds. Conjugated dienes like 1,3-butadiene are used in the production of synthetic rubber. The conjugated structure allows for polymerization, leading to long chains that exhibit rubber-like properties.

blocks.prompt: a) Draw the structure of simple conjugated dienes such as Buta-1,3-diene.
blocks.explanation: Buta-1,3-diene: CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂. Its four sp² carbon atoms lie in one plane, with the double bonds C1=C2 and C3=C4 joined by the single bond C2–C3 (see the drawing in answer b).

blocks.prompt: b) Illustrate the delocalization of electrons in conjugated dienes.
blocks.explanation: Each of the four carbon atoms has a p orbital. These p orbitals, from carbon 1 to carbon 4, are all parallel and close together, so they overlap continuously above and below the chain, and the four π electrons spread over the whole system instead of staying in two separate bonds. This delocalization lowers the energy, so the diene is more stable than two isolated double bonds, and an electrophile can also add at both ends (1,4-addition).

answer_figure.alt: Two-part answer diagram: (a) the full structural formula of buta-1,3-diene, four carbons numbered 1 to 4, C1=C2 and C3=C4 double bonds, a C2-C3 single bond and six H atoms; (b) the four carbons in a straight line, one p orbital above and below each carbon, and one long purple pi electron cloud above and below all the p orbitals, extending from C1 to C4.
answer_figure.caption: Answer diagram: the structure of buta-1,3-diene and the delocalization of its four π electrons (from C1 to C4).
answer_figure.long_description: At the top is the structural formula of buta-1,3-diene, CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂: four carbon atoms in one plane, two double bonds (C1=C2, C3=C4) and a single bond between them (C2–C3). Below are the same four carbon atoms, each with one p orbital (green lobes). These are all parallel, so they overlap with one another and form one continuous purple π cloud above and below the chain from C1 to C4. The four π electrons are therefore not confined to two separate bonds but spread (delocalised) over the whole system.
